definition: A reduction or temporary suspension of rent, usually granted when the landlord fails to make required repairs or the unit becomes partially uninhabitable.
Items left behind by a tenant after moving out or vacating the rental unit.
When a tenant leaves a rental unit without notice or intent to return while still under lease obligations.
If you break the lease, this clause makes all remaining rent immediately due rather than month by month. Not enforceable in all jurisdictions.
A rental unit designed or modified to accommodate individuals with disabilities, including mobility and sensory accessibility features.
A state of being behind on payments such as rent or utilities.
A rental agreement where the tenant accepts the property in its current condition without required repairs.
A non-lease occupant who pays to live in a unit but has limited legal tenant rights.
A licensed professional who helps negotiate rental agreements between landlords and tenants.
Official approval confirming a property is safe and legal for habitation.
A shared recreational or social facility within a residential complex.
Shared spaces within a property available for use by all tenants.
Areas of the apartment complex — such as the gym, laundry rooms, clubhouse and outdoor spaces — that are for common use. Every renter in the complex is allowed to use the common area.
Legal principles defining rights and obligations under housing law and landlord-tenant relationships.
When a landlord’s failure to maintain habitable conditions forces a tenant to leave, potentially releasing the tenant from lease obligations.
A legally binding agreement between parties that creates enforceable obligations.
A person who signs a lease agreeing to be responsible for rent if the tenant fails to pay.
A tenant who shares equal rights and responsibilities under a lease agreement with other tenants.
A binding promise in the lease — either something a party will do (positive covenant) or will not do (restrictive covenant), such as not running a business from the unit.
A record of a person's borrowing and repayment behavior used to assess financial reliability.
Failure by either party to meet a contract obligation — usually the tenant not paying rent. Default can trigger late fees, penalties, or eviction proceedings.
The process of investigating and verifying information before entering an agreement or transaction.
A structure used as a residential home.
A legal remedy allowing landlords in some jurisdictions to seize tenant property to recover unpaid rent.
A right allowing a third party to use part of the property for a specific purpose, such as a utility company accessing pipes through shared corridors.
Conditions, notice requirements, and penalties for ending a lease before its agreed expiration date.
Money held by a neutral third party until a condition is met. Security deposits are often held in escrow to protect both tenant and landlord from disputes.
A signed statement confirming the lease terms are as written and no disputes exist. Often requested by banks or buyers when the property is sold or refinanced.
Actions taken by a landlord that prevent a tenant from accessing their rental unit, such as changing locks or shutting off utilities.
The legal process of removing a tenant from a rental property for lease violations or nonpayment.
A federal law prohibiting housing discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, disability, familial status, or national origin.
A tenant's right to renew or re-lease a unit before it is offered to others.
A lease agreement with a defined start and end date.
The process where a lender takes ownership of a property due to the landlord’s failure to meet mortgage obligations.
Excuses either party from obligations when an extraordinary event occurs — natural disaster, pandemic, or government shutdown — that makes performance impossible.
A temporary visitor to a rental unit who is not a tenant or occupant.
A third party who agrees to cover rent if the tenant defaults. The guarantor is legally liable for the lease obligations.
The tenant pays a single flat rent and the landlord covers all operating expenses — utilities, insurance, property tax, maintenance.
Your legal right to a safe, clean, livable home. Landlords must maintain plumbing, heating, and structural integrity. Failure may let you withhold rent depending on local law.
A tenant who remains in the property after the lease expires without signing a renewal. Landlords can either accept this (creating a month-to-month tenancy) or pursue eviction.
Heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems in a building.
A clause requiring you to protect the landlord from financial loss caused by your actions. If a guest is injured in your unit and sues, you — not the landlord — cover the costs.
An agreement where one party compensates another for certain losses or damages.
The legal authority of a court or government to hear and decide cases.
When multiple tenants sign a lease, each is individually responsible for the full rent. If one tenant stops paying, others can be pursued for the full amount.
A shared fund contributed by co-tenants for shared household expenses.
A hidden flaw not visible during inspection — mold behind walls, faulty wiring, structural damage. Undisclosed latent defects may give you legal grounds for compensation.
The property owner or authorized agent who leases residential property to tenants.
The official contact details of the landlord or property manager responsible for the rental unit.
A formal contract outlining rent, rules, duration, and responsibilities between landlord and tenant.
Transferring your entire lease to a new tenant who assumes all rights and obligations, typically requiring landlord approval.
The official date when a lease begins and the tenant may take possession of the unit.
The fixed duration of the rental agreement — typically 6 or 12 months. Breaking the lease early usually incurs penalties specified in the contract.
The tenant who leases the property.
The landlord or property owner who leases the property.
Legal responsibility for damages, debts, or violations.
A legal hold on a property by a third party (bank, contractor) who is owed money. A lien on your building could affect your tenancy if the landlord defaults.
A pre-agreed sum specified in the lease as compensation for a specific breach, such as early termination. Courts may void these if the amount is punitive.
A dispute resolution process involving a neutral third party.
A property design combining residential, commercial, or office spaces within the same building or area.
A rental arrangement with no fixed end date, automatically renewing each month. Either party can typically terminate with 30 days written notice.
The tenant pays base rent plus some or all operating costs. A triple net (NNN) lease has the tenant paying rent, utilities, insurance, and property taxes.
A legal contract that prevents parties from sharing confidential information.
Minor deterioration expected from ordinary use — small scuffs, faded paint, worn carpet. Landlords cannot deduct this from your security deposit; only damage beyond this qualifies.
A formal written notice from the landlord demanding the tenant vacate. The required notice period varies by jurisdiction — typically 30 to 90 days.
A tenant’s formal written notice informing the landlord of intent to move out.
Replacing one party in a contract with another, releasing the original party from obligations.
A lease rule prohibiting behavior that interferes with other tenants' quiet enjoyment.
The number of parking spaces available per unit or tenant in a property.
A refundable fee intended to cover damages caused by pets in a rental unit.
Illegal discrimination in housing based on protected characteristics.
A partial month's rent calculated based on the number of days occupied when moving in or out mid-month.
Your right to use the property peacefully without interference from the landlord or anyone claiming ownership. Violation of this right may void the lease.
Payment made by a tenant to a landlord for use of a property.
Monthly rent amount and any additional charges such as utilities, parking, pets, or HOA fees.
Laws that limit how much rent can be increased, depending on local regulations and property type.
A system that regulates rent increases annually while still allowing controlled adjustments.
The continuation of a lease agreement after its initial term ends.
Procedures for maintenance requests, landlord entry notice requirements, and emergency repair protocols.
A legally binding contract between landlord and tenant defining rental terms and responsibilities.
A document completed by prospective tenants to evaluate eligibility for renting a property.
Rules governing tenant behavior including smoking, pets, subletting, and prohibited activities.
A residential space leased by a tenant from a property owner.
Whether tenants must maintain insurance coverage, including minimum coverage amounts and proof requirements.
The landlord's right to enter your unit. Most jurisdictions require 24–48 hours written notice except in genuine emergencies.
A person who shares a rental unit with another tenant.
The process of evaluating a tenant’s credit, rental, and background history.
Money paid upfront, held by the landlord to cover unpaid rent or damages beyond normal wear and tear.
A lease where rent increases at scheduled intervals.
Renting your unit to another person while you remain the primary tenant. Most leases either forbid this or require written landlord approval.
If your insurer pays out a claim, this clause lets them sue the responsible party on your behalf to recover that money, preventing you from double-collecting.
The duration of a lease agreement.
A rental agreement with no fixed term, terminable by either party with proper notice.
The duration of a rental agreement, such as month-to-month or fixed-term leases with defined start and end dates.
Full legal names and identifying details of all tenants and additional occupants listed on a lease.
Legal protections ensuring tenants can safely and lawfully occupy a rental unit.
The ending of a lease agreement by either party.
A court process used by landlords to legally remove a tenant who refuses to vacate after proper notice.
Recurring service costs such as electricity, water, gas, internet, and waste removal.
The percentage of rental units that are unoccupied in a property or market.
The voluntary relinquishment of a known contractual right, such as consistently accepting late rent without penalty.
Normal deterioration of a property due to everyday use.
